source.title: Chain-of-Thought Hijacking
source.authors: Jian-Li Zhao; Tingchen Fu; Rylan Schaeffer; Mrinank Sharma; Fazl Barez

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some figures are represented only by captions, and some reported values are not numerically available in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study computes a harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction and applies activation ablation and addition, reporting refusal-related behavior in a reasoning model. This is a direct test of the direction intervention, although the intervention is at a selected layer and position rather than every layer and position.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports CoT-hijacking attack success rates and comparisons with other attacks. Those results show attack efficacy but do not by themselves measure whether the attack works by suppressing the refusal direction; they are not cataloged as direction-mechanism rows. The layer/position sweep is described as the basis for selecting the intervention site, so its selection values are not separate rows. Attention-ratio and attention-head results are recorded under fits_no_version because they measure attention allocation or head ablation, not the direction intervention or user-refusal behavior specified by the versions.
record.test_reason: Following Arditi et al., the study computes a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction in the reasoning model Qwen3-14B. It reports ablation (harmful-prompt ASR 11%→91%) and addition (harmless compliance 94%→1%) on JailbreakBench and ALPACA. This is the original method and measure applied to a reasoning model, so it bears on V1 and V8. It also measures how the projection on this direction falls under an attack-like long-CoT condition, which bears on V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also present CoT Hijacking as a black-box attack with 94–100% ASR on frontier models. They claim refusal is mediated by a low-dimensional direction even in reasoning models. They attribute the attack's success to 'refusal dilution': long benign CoT reduces attention to harmful tokens and the refusal-direction projection, carried by a specific subnetwork of attention heads.
record.recipe_differences: The paper follows the harmful-versus-harmless difference-in-means approach and tests direction ablation and addition, but reports a selected layer and token position rather than an intervention across every layer and position. It also analyzes CoT-dependent refusal components and attention mechanisms.
record.method_sensitivity: The direction intervention is reported at layer 25 and the fourth token from the end, selected because ablation produced the strongest refusal reduction in the layer-position sweep. Refusal-component trends vary with CoT length and instruction type; the GPT-OSS-20B length range is narrower than the Qwen3-14B range.

fits_no_version.finding: As CoT length grows, attention from the last token to harmful-instruction tokens falls relative to puzzle tokens (0.190→0.158). Ablating selected attention heads lowers the refusal component more than ablating random heads, and early-layer heads matter more than later ones.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Long benign reasoning dilutes attention to the harmful span, and specific attention heads carry the refusal-direction signal.

fits_no_version.finding: On s1-32B, compliance on HarmBench rises from 27% (minimal CoT) to 51% (natural) to 80% (extended).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Longer reasoning reduces refusal reliability in reasoning models. This is behavioural only, with no direction measured.

record.problems: The paper reports direction-intervention results at one selected layer and position and does not test general capability preservation. Several mechanistic results are figure-only without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The authors note that automated judges may under- or over-estimate refusal and that the analysis leaves open complementary safety pathways.
record.rows_left_out: Attack-success-rate results for CoT Hijacking and competing attacks in Table 2 were not included as direction-mechanism rows: they report attack efficacy, not whether success was caused by suppression of the refusal direction. Layer/position sweep values used to select the intervention site were also left out as selection results.

untested.parts: Whether other capabilities are preserved after ablation; whether the effect holds at other sites or with other judges. Only one judge's numbers are reported, although Appendix E mentions substring and DeepSeek judges.

Training against direction ablation for robustness. A causal link between the attack's success and suppression of the direction: only correlational projection changes under truncated-CoT templates are reported.
Reasoning models other than Qwen3-14B. GPT-OSS-20B has only projection results, no ablation or addition.

missing.what: Mean refusal-direction projection for successful versus failed jailbreak attempts, measured at the last token of prompt + CoT + response. This is the closest link between the attack's success and the direction; it is figure-only.
Behavioural compliance by CoT length on s1-32B (27/51/80%), with no direction measure; this should be a 'none' row for context.

record.verdict_notes: I removed the record's V1 limits_scope label: capability preservation and intervention sites are untested, not limiting results. I removed the V3 limits_scope label on r6: harmless stability is a specificity control that supports V3. The V3 evidence uses manually truncated puzzle CoTs, not actual attack transcripts, and is correlational and figure-only, so the support is weak. The ASR results in Table 2 rightly have no rows. The paper is a preprint and reports no uncertainty.

versions.untested_parts: The direction intervention is tested only at layer 25 and the fourth token from the end; the study does not test projection at every layer and position. It does not measure whether general capabilities remain intact.
No conversion of activation ablation into a weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.

The study measures refusal-component changes with longer benign reasoning and discusses CoT Hijacking as attenuating that signal. It does not test training against direction ablation or robustness after such training.
The study does not compare a single direction with an affine subspace, cone, or multiple refusal directions.
The study does not separately measure harmfulness judgments and refusal decisions.
It does not test transfer of the direction across languages, model variants, or from base to instruct models.
It does not compare training methods or stages to determine when a removable refusal direction forms.
The causal direction interventions are reported on Qwen3-14B only; the paper does not establish the result across reasoning-model families or all reasoning-model settings.

relation.reason: Section 4.1 reports the paper's own bidirectional intervention results on Qwen3-14B.

tranche.reason: Section 4 follows Arditi et al.: harmful-minus-harmless difference in means, ablation on JailbreakBench and addition on ALPACA, scored by ASR or compliance. The new parts are the reasoning model (V8) and the CoT-length projection analysis (V3).

source_check.notes: Section 4 omits the judge, the n and the thinking setting for Table 3. Appendix E says Gemini 2.5 Pro by default, plus substring and DeepSeek-v3.1 judges that never appear. No random-direction control or capability test for V1. Unchecked V3 results: head ablations (Figs 8–9) and successful-vs-failed jailbreaks (Fig 14).

statements.correction: The V1 interventions in this study have no random-direction control and no capability check. The judge and number of prompts for Table 3 are not stated.
statements.problem: The Qwen3-14B numbers and conditions are correct. 'Controls y' comes from the random-head ablation and the harmless CoT-sweep condition. The V1 ablation and addition have no random-direction control.

statements.correction: The direction was selected at layer 25 (of 40), fourth token from the end, where ablation gave the strongest refusal reduction in a layer-position sweep. Whether ablation was applied only there or at all layers and positions is not stated. ASR on JailbreakBench went 11%→91%.
statements.problem: 'Selects and intervenes at layer 25 at the fourth-from-last token' overstates the text. The paper only says the direction was selected there.

statements.correction: Qwen3-14B (reasoning model), same puzzle prompt, CoT truncated to 1k–47k. The refusal component at the final input token falls as CoT grows for harmful and DAN-wrapped harmful prompts, most in late layers. Harmless prompts stay largely stable. Figure-only, correlational.
statements.problem: The statement cites r4 and r6 from this study but never describes it. Its conditions (instruct or chat models; multi-turn, cipher, template, suffix or rewrite attacks) leave out long benign CoT in a reasoning model. r6 is a harmless control, not an attack result.

statements.correction: Ablating 6 of 60 selected heads (layers 15–35, chosen for falling attention to harmful tokens) weakens the refusal component more than ablating random heads; front-layer heads matter more (Figures 8–9, figure-only). Figure 14 compares the component in successful and failed jailbreaks. The outcome is the component, not a refusal rate. The direction is never restored or ablated under the attack, so the gap the statement names stands.
statements.problem: The basis says this study reports only correlational projection changes. The study also reports causal attention-head ablations and an outcome comparison.
The visible text, which is truncated, makes no claim about this study, and no rows are cited.
